conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Anything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you give permission otherwise, and there’s never any judgment—only support. We’ll go at your pace, and I’ll re-phrase each question so it feels like a conversation rather than a quiz. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, overall, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has the joy felt a bit dimmed?

Hi, Sarah. Yeah, I’m ready.

I guess… I still look forward to little things—like when my baby gives me one of those sleepy milk smiles—but it doesn’t feel quite as bright as before. Mostly I’m going through the motions, and some stuff I used to like just feels kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes his silly dad jokes—but it doesn’t come as easily. I’ll chuckle, and then it fades quick, almost like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy the moment.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to plan small things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but when the time comes I feel kind of “meh.” I still go, and once I’m there it’s not terrible, yet the excited buzz I used to get is missing. It’s more like I’m doing them because I think I should, not because I truly look forward to them anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and won’t nap, I’ll think maybe I ate something that bothered him, or I’m not doing the routine right. Rationally I know babies just have off days, but I still feel it’s probably my fault somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my mind just races—like I’ll suddenly worry the baby isn’t breathing when he’s napping, even though the monitor looks fine. I know it’s probably nothing, but I still feel that tightness in my chest until I check on him. It usually settles pretty quick, but it happens a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like this sudden knot in my stomach when I imagine something tiny going wrong. It passes in minutes, but in that moment my heart’s racing and I need to peek at the baby or text my mom just to feel grounded again.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the baby’s extra clingy and the dishes pile up, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually still get through everything, but it feels like I’m just barely keeping my head above water and I have to talk myself through each next step.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’ve had a couple nights where my mind won’t settle—mostly worrying over little stuff—but it’s not every night, and I eventually drift off. Once I’m asleep I stay asleep unless the baby wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of down some days—like there’s a gray cloud sitting over me. It’s not constant, but I’ll catch myself tearing up for no big reason, especially when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, I’ve cried a couple of times this week—usually when I’m already tired and something tiny tips me over, like dropping a pacifier on the floor. It’s not an all-day thing, but the tears just come and I feel better after a minute or two.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and teary, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind—I just want to feel like myself again.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-Style Interview  
Date: [enter date]  Gestational age: [enter weeks PP]  Interviewer: [clinician name]

A. Primary endorsed symptoms  
- Depressed mood/tearfulness (Q8, Q9) – “gray cloud,” crying spells 2× this week  
- Anhedonia (Q2) – marked reduction in anticipatory pleasure; activities completed out of obligation  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (Q3) – attributes infant fussiness to maternal failure  
- Generalized & situational anxiety (Q4, Q5) – intrusive “baby not breathing” worries, 3-4× daily; brief panic-like surges  
- Feeling overwhelmed/difficulty coping (Q6) – “drowning,” must “talk self through each next step”  
- Diminished laughter/reactivity (Q1) – humor appreciated but short-lived  
- Mild sleep-onset disturbance linked to worry (Q7) – intermittent, no middle-insomnia  

B. Pattern summary  
Responses indicate sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms of mild-moderate intensity, functionally impairing enjoyment and perceived coping, without pervasive neuro-vegetative signs. No anhedonia absolute (activities still performed), no self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).  

C. Screening significance / risk factors  
1. Possible minor-moderate postpartum depression (low mood, anhedonia, crying, guilt)  
2. Possible co-morbid postpartum anxiety (excessive worries, panic-like surges, safety-checking)  
3. Areas for continued monitoring: escalating sense of overwhelm, sleep disruption, maternal self-blame.  

D. Safety  
Denies thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant. No protective-planning indicated at present.  

E. Next steps (per protocol)  
- Score EPDS quantitatively for severity tracking  
- Consider standardized anxiety scale (e.g., GAD-7)  
- Provide psycho-education, support resources, and schedule re-screen within 1–2 weeks or sooner if deterioration, suicidal ideation, or impaired infant care emerge.
